newsitem.title: USA: SEC wants to turn legal jargon into plain English.
newsitem.headline: SEC wants to turn legal jargon into plain English.

text.p: In effort to make business information easier to understand, the Securities and Exchange Commission proposed Monday that company prospectuses be written in simple, clear language instead of legal jargon.
The proposed "plain English" regulation was approved unanimously by the four commission members. A vote on final approval will be taken after a two-month comment period.

"Whenever you have something of this magnitude that affects investors across the country ... it's a major milestone," said Nancy Smith, director of the SEC's Office of Investor Education and Assistance.

The proposal would require the cover page, summary and "risk factors" sections in prospectuses and all other documents filed with the agency to be written in the active voice using short sentences with unambiguous everyday words.

Many lawyers and corporate officers support the proposal, SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt told a meeting of the commission, adding that they agreed it was time to "jettison the legalese and speak plainly to investors."
"They understand that plain English does not mean 'dumbing down' ...," Levitt said. "It just means presenting complex information clearly."

Describing the reforms as cultural changes, Levitt said the SEC would not act as "grammatical policemen" in pursuing violators of the "plain English" rule. But another SEC official said documents could be sent back for a rewrite.
The SEC proposal follows a pilot program by a number companies, including Bell Atlantic Corp., Baltimore Gas and Electric Co. and ITT Corp.
The companies have filed "plain English" merger documents, shelf offerings and proxy statements with the SEC without added expense, SEC officials said.
The idea had been criticized by some corporate lawyers who said plain English was not precise enough and could lead to increased misinterpretation and liability for issuers of the documents.

But Baltimore Gas Associate General Counsel Susan Wolf told the commission there was no greater risk of liability by using ordinary language, saying the documents are easier to read and actually subject to less misinterpretation.

The commission also issued the draft of a 57-page handbook with suggestions and tips on how to create plain English documents. The handbook is currently under review and is expected to be issued later this year.
